title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how AI education can be made more accessible in K-12 classrooms by integrating AI concepts into existing core subjects, rather than treating AI as a standalone computing topic. The authors focus on the challenge that many teachers lack AI experience and need practical support to design usable, classroom-ready lessons.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators and researchers. Participants first learned basic AI concepts and tools, then completed pre-work and group design activities to create integrated lesson plans for non-computing subjects, including social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop included presentations, discussion, card sorting, exemplar curriculum review, and collaborative lesson-plan development.

The paper reports qualitative analysis of workshop transcripts, questionnaires, and design artifacts, along with descriptive pre/post self-ratings of AI familiarity and confidence. The authors conclude that teachers value curriculum supports for evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that AI can be integrated through data use, student reflection, and ethics discussions. They argue that co-design with teachers can produce implementable integrated AI curricula and highlight the need for scaffolding to help teachers teach AI ethics confidently.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design / descriptive workshop study with pre-post self-report surveys, not a causal evaluation of a teacher-facing AI intervention. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically clear, but it provides exploratory evidence rather than high-credibility impact estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical design implications for integrating AI into K-12 curricula and reports increased teacher familiarity/confidence, but these are self-reported and not tied to student outcomes or a controlled intervention. Impact is therefore plausible but modest and uncertain.
